options.text: In the cookie itself
On the server, found by the session id in the cookie
In the URL
In the browser's localStorage

questions.explanation: The cookie holds only an opaque id. The state lives in memory, Redis or a database on the server, which is also why a session can be revoked instantly.

questions.text: Why must a session id be long and random?

options.text: So the cookie is easy to read
So it cannot be guessed or enumerated by an attacker
To make the cookie smaller
So it sorts well in the database

questions.explanation: Anyone who guesses a valid id becomes that user. Use a cryptographically secure random generator and enough bits that guessing is hopeless.

sql-joins-and-grouping.title: SQL joins, grouping and NULL
sql-joins-and-grouping.description: Which join to pick, how WHERE and HAVING differ, and the NULL and join-grain traps that quietly return wrong numbers.

questions.text: You need a report of every customer and how many orders each has, including customers with zero orders. Which join fits?

options.text: INNER JOIN from customers to orders
CROSS JOIN from customers to orders
LEFT JOIN from customers to orders
INNER JOIN from orders to customers

questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and fills the order columns with NULL when nothing matches. An INNER JOIN, in either direction, drops customers with no orders, so the report silently understates the customer list.

questions.text: Why does SELECT c.name, count(*) AS n FROM ... WHERE n > 2 fail, while ORDER BY n works?

options.text: ORDER BY is the only clause allowed to use aliases, by the SQL standard's syntax rules
WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet; ORDER BY runs after SELECT
n is a reserved word, which only works in ORDER BY
WHERE runs after GROUP BY, and grouped rows cannot be filtered

questions.explanation: The logical order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. An alias is created at the SELECT step, and the aggregate does not exist until grouping. Option d has it backwards: WHERE runs before GROUP BY.

questions.text: You want customers who have placed at least 3 orders. Where does the condition go?

options.text: In HAVING count(o.id) >= 3, after GROUP BY
In WHERE count(o.id) >= 3
In the ON clause of the join
In ORDER BY count(o.id) >= 3

questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation, which is exactly what a count threshold needs.

questions.text: A teammate writes: SELECT c.name, o.total_cents FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.total_cents > 1000. Customers with no orders vanish. Why?

options.text: LEFT JOIN only keeps customers who have at least one order over the limit
The database rewrites every LEFT JOIN into a RIGHT JOIN when WHERE is present
total_cents must be indexed for a LEFT JOIN to keep unmatched rows
Unmatched rows have NULL in total_cents, and WHERE total_cents > 1000 rejects NULL, turning the join back into an inner join

questions.explanation: WHERE runs after the join and a comparison with NULL is never true, so the preserved no-match rows are filtered out. Put the condition on the optional table in the ON clause instead (ON ... AND o.total_cents > 1000).

questions.text: After customers LEFT JOIN orders, grouped by customer, which expressions give 0 for a customer with no orders? Select all that apply.

options.text: count(o.id)
count(*)
COALESCE(sum(o.total_cents), 0)
sum(o.total_cents)

questions.explanation: count(column) skips NULLs, so the placeholder row counts as zero, and COALESCE turns the NULL sum into 0. count(*) counts the placeholder row and returns 1, and a bare sum() over only NULLs returns NULL.

questions.text: WHERE deleted_at = NULL returns the rows where deleted_at is not set.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: NULL means unknown, so NULL = NULL is itself NULL, not true, and the query matches nothing. Use deleted_at IS NULL.

questions.text: A query on tables of 1,000 and 2,000 rows returns about 2,000,000 rows and hangs. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A missing index on the primary key
A missing or wrong join condition, which produced a cross join
Using INNER JOIN instead of EXISTS
Using ORDER BY without LIMIT

questions.explanation: Without a join condition every left row pairs with every right row, so the row count is left times right. A missing index makes a query slow but does not change how many rows come back.

questions.text: After joining customers to orders, summing a per-customer column such as credit_limit counts each customer's value once per order.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The join changes the grain of the result to one row per order, so a customer with three orders appears three times and their credit limit is triple-counted. Summing an order-level value such as total_cents is fine.

system-design-availability-latency-and-s.title: Availability, latency, throughput and single points of failure
system-design-availability-latency-and-s.description: The nines, availability in series and in parallel, Little's Law, percentile latency and finding single points of failure.

questions.text: A service promises 99.9% availability over a year. About how much downtime does that allow?

options.text: About 53 minutes
About 3.7 days
About 36 hours
About 8.8 hours

questions.explanation: 0.1% of 8,760 hours in a year is about 8.8 hours. About 53 minutes is 99.99% (four nines), and about 3.7 days is 99%.

questions.text: A request must pass through a web tier and then a database, in series. Each is 99.9% available and they fail independently. What is the availability of the pair?

options.text: About 99.8%
About 99.95%

questions.explanation: In series you multiply: 0.999 x 0.999 = 0.998, so each extra required component lowers the total. The pair can never be better than its weakest part. 99.99% would be the result for two redundant copies, not a chain.

questions.text: Two identical servers each have 99% availability, fail independently, and either one can serve all traffic. What is the availability of the pair?
questions.explanation: The service is down only when both are down: 0.01 x 0.01 = 0.0001, so availability is 99.99%. This assumes independent failures and working failover, which is why two instances in one rack or behind one shared dependency do not get this benefit.

questions.text: By Little's Law, how many requests are in flight on average when a service handles 5,000 requests per second and each takes 50 ms?
questions.explanation: Concurrency = throughput x latency = 5,000 per second x 0.05 s = 250. The tempting 100,000 comes from dividing by 0.05 instead of multiplying, and 25 comes from treating 50 ms as 0.005 s.

questions.text: Which of these are single points of failure? Select all that apply.

options.text: One Redis instance that holds the sessions for every app server
Four stateless app servers spread across two availability zones
One database primary with no standby or replica
Two load balancers sharing a virtual IP, with automatic failover

questions.explanation: If the only Redis or the only database primary dies, everything that depends on it stops, however many app servers sit in front. Redundant stateless servers and a failover pair of load balancers are the fixes, not the problem.

questions.text: A dashboard shows an average latency of 80 ms and a p99 of 300 ms. What does the p99 figure mean?

options.text: 99% of requests finished in 300 ms or less, and the slowest 1% took longer
The average of the slowest 1% of requests is 300 ms
300 ms is the longest any request has taken
Requests are 99% likely to take exactly 300 ms

questions.explanation: A percentile is a cut-off: p99 is the value that 99% of requests stay under. The tail can be far worse than the cut-off, and the average hides it, which is why latency targets are written as percentiles.

questions.text: Shortening the time it takes to recover from a failure can raise availability as much as making failures less frequent.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Availability is roughly MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR), so cutting the repair time raises it just as lengthening the time between failures does. Automated failover that turns a 30-minute outage into 30 seconds is often easier than preventing the failure.

questions.text: If one server handles 1,000 requests per second, 10 servers will always handle 10,000 requests per second.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Scaling is linear only when nothing is shared. A shared database, lock or other serial part caps the gain (Amdahl's Law), so the added servers deliver less than 10x.

tcp-ip-dns-ports-and-nat.title: TCP, DNS, ports and NAT
tcp-ip-dns-ports-and-nat.description: How a name becomes an address, how a connection reaches the right program, and what the failure messages tell you.

questions.text: A client tries to connect to a server's port and gets "Connection refused" almost instantly. What is the most likely situation?

options.text: A firewall is silently dropping the SYN packets
The server's host is powered off
The host is reachable, but nothing is listening on that port
The domain name failed to resolve

questions.explanation: A host with no listening socket on the port answers with a TCP reset, which the client reports at once as refused. A silent drop or a dead host gives no reply, so the client waits and times out; a DNS failure would never get as far as a connection.

questions.text: Seeing many sockets in TIME-WAIT on a busy client is a sign that the application is leaking connections.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: TIME-WAIT is how TCP lets a recently closed connection linger briefly to catch stray packets, and it clears on its own. A growing pile of CLOSE-WAIT is the one that usually points to an application that forgets to close sockets.

questions.text: A service answers curl http://127.0.0.1:8080 on its own machine, but other hosts cannot connect. Which explanation and check fit best?

options.text: It is bound to 127.0.0.1 only; ss -tlnp shows 127.0.0.1:8080 instead of 0.0.0.0:8080
TCP does not allow more than one client per port; ss -tan shows the active client
Port 8080 is a privileged port; ls -l shows who owns the binary
The DNS TTL is too long; dig +trace shows the delay

questions.explanation: A socket bound to the loopback address is invisible to every other host, and ss -tlnp shows the address it is bound to. One listening port serves many clients, 8080 is not below 1024, and DNS is not involved when the address is already known.

questions.text: dig example.com returns the correct IP, but curl example.com connects to a different machine. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the TCP three-way handshake is being retransmitted
Whether the server certificate has expired
Whether the DNS record is a CNAME or an A record
Whether /etc/hosts has an entry for that name

questions.explanation: Applications resolve names through the system resolver, which normally reads /etc/hosts before asking DNS, while dig always queries a DNS server. When dig and getent or curl disagree, a hosts-file override is the first suspect.

questions.text: Which statements about DNS are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A CNAME record maps a name to another name, which the resolver then looks up
An A record maps a name to an IPv6 address
Lowering a record's TTL before a planned change makes the change take effect sooner
A DNS TTL is a hop counter that routers decrement

questions.explanation: CNAME is an alias, and a short TTL means caches refetch sooner, so operators lower it ahead of a migration. IPv6 addresses live in AAAA records, and the hop counter is the unrelated TTL field in the IP header; a DNS TTL is a caching lifetime in seconds.

questions.text: A host is configured as 10.0.5.40/29. Which of these addresses is on the same local network?
questions.explanation: A /29 has 8 addresses, so blocks start at multiples of 8 and this one spans 10.0.5.40 to 10.0.5.47. 10.0.5.39 and 10.0.5.48 sit in the neighbouring blocks, and 10.0.6.41 is a different third octet entirely, so the host would send those to its gateway.

questions.text: A container on a private address behind NAT can usually open connections to the internet, but an outside host cannot start a connection to it unless a port forward is configured.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: NAT creates its translation entry when the inside host sends the first packet out, so replies can find their way back. With no entry and a non-routable private address, unsolicited inbound traffic has nowhere to go until a port forward (destination NAT) maps it.

questions.text: Which workloads fit UDP better than TCP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Transferring a file where every byte must arrive intact
A DNS query and its short response
A database client talking to its server
A live voice call where a late packet is useless

questions.explanation: UDP skips the handshake and retransmission, which suits small request/response exchanges and real-time media where timeliness beats completeness. Files and database traffic need TCP's reliable, ordered delivery.

tls-and-https-basics.title: TLS and HTTPS basics
tls-and-https-basics.description: What TLS does and does not protect, how certificates are checked, and where HTTPS ends in a real deployment.

questions.text: Which three guarantees does TLS give an HTTPS connection?

options.text: Compression, caching and load balancing
Encryption, integrity and server authentication
Authorization, rate limiting and logging
Anonymity, availability and data-at-rest protection

questions.explanation: TLS keeps the bytes unreadable to eavesdroppers, detects tampering, and proves the server is who its certificate says. It does not hide who you connected to and does not protect data once it is stored or after TLS ends.

questions.text: If a site presents a valid certificate and the browser shows a padlock, you can be sure the site is honest and safe.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The padlock means the connection is encrypted and the server is who its certificate says it is. A scam site can have a perfectly valid certificate for its own domain.

questions.text: When a client verifies a server's certificate during the TLS handshake, which checks does it make? Select all that apply.

options.text: The chain of signatures leads up to a root CA in its trust store
The hostname it asked for is covered by the certificate
The website's content has been reviewed and is safe
The current date is inside the certificate's validity period

questions.explanation: Chain of trust, hostname match and validity dates are what the client can actually check. Nothing in the certificate says anything about whether the site's content is safe.

questions.text: All your API clients suddenly fail with "certificate has expired". Which command shows the certificate's validity dates for a host?

options.text: curl -k https://example.com/
dig example.com TXT
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com, piped to openssl x509 -noout -dates
ss -tlnp on the client

questions.explanation: openssl s_client fetches the certificate and x509 -noout -dates prints notBefore and notAfter. curl -k would just skip verification and hide the problem, and the other commands inspect DNS or local sockets.

questions.text: A network observer between a client and an HTTPS site can typically still see which of these? Select all that apply.

options.text: The destination IP address
The value of the Authorization header
The JSON request body
The server name sent in the TLS handshake (SNI), in a typical setup

questions.explanation: TLS hides the HTTP content: headers, cookies, tokens and bodies. It does not hide the fact of the connection, so the IP address and normally the SNI hostname stay visible.

questions.text: TLS is terminated at your load balancer, and the app behind it sees plain http:// requests. How can the app learn that the client originally used HTTPS?

options.text: From an X-Forwarded-Proto header set by the proxy
From the port number on the app's own socket
From the TLS certificate in the request
It cannot be known, so apps must always redirect to HTTPS themselves

questions.explanation: The proxy adds the original scheme as X-Forwarded-Proto, which the app should trust only from a proxy it controls. The certificate and the original TLS session never reach the app once TLS has ended at the balancer.

questions.text: What does the header Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 tell a browser?

options.text: The certificate will be renewed automatically in a year
Cookies should be encrypted at rest for a year
Session tokens expire after a year
For the next year, only connect to this site over HTTPS, even if the user types http://

questions.explanation: HSTS makes the browser refuse plain HTTP for the site, which defeats SSL-stripping downgrade attacks. It has nothing to do with certificate renewal or token lifetimes, and it only makes sense once HTTPS works everywhere on the site.

questions.text: Turning off certificate verification (curl -k, or verify=False in an HTTP library) in production code is acceptable because the traffic is still encrypted.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Without verification you no longer know who you are talking to, so a man-in-the-middle can present their own certificate and read everything. -k is for debugging a certificate problem only.

tokens-attention-transformers.title: Tokens, attention and transformers
tokens-attention-transformers.description: What a language model actually sees, and the attention mechanics inside a transformer: Q/K/V, scaling, masks and heads.

questions.text: What does a language model actually receive as input?

options.text: The raw characters of the text, one at a time
One ID per word, using a dictionary of every English word
Integer IDs of tokens, which are chunks of text from a fixed learned vocabulary
The text plus a separate list of its grammatical parts

questions.explanation: A tokenizer maps text to vocabulary entries, and the model only sees their integer IDs. A token can be a whole word, a word piece or a single character or byte, so it is not the same as a word.

questions.text: A sentence in Hindi or Japanese usually costs about the same number of tokens as the English sentence with the same meaning.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Tokenizers trained mostly on English text split non-Latin scripts into more, smaller tokens. The exact ratio depends on the language and the tokenizer (2-3 times is common, and it can be higher), but it is rarely close to 1. That raises both cost and latency for the same content.

questions.text: Why are queries, keys and values computed with three separate learned projections instead of using the token vectors X directly for all three?

options.text: It makes the matrices smaller so attention runs faster
Using X as both query and key makes the score matrix symmetric and biases each token toward attending to itself, so the model cannot learn directional relations between tokens
Softmax only works if the inputs come from a linear projection
It is needed to make the output the same length as the input

questions.explanation: If Q = K = X, the scores are X times X-transpose: the score from token i to token j always equals the score from j to i, and a token's dot product with itself (its squared length) tends to dominate its row, so each token is biased toward attending to itself. Separate Wq and Wk give each token a 'what I look for' vector and a different 'what I offer' vector, which removes the symmetry and lets the model learn which other tokens matter.

questions.text: Why are attention scores divided by sqrt(d_k) before the softmax?

options.text: Dot products grow with the dimension, so large scores would saturate the softmax and leave almost no gradient to learn from
It makes the weights for each row sum to exactly 1
It hides future tokens from the current position
It reduces the number of parameters in the layer

questions.explanation: The spread of dot products between random vectors scales with sqrt(d), so unscaled scores make softmax nearly one-hot and its gradient tiny. Softmax already normalises each row to 1, so that is not the reason for the scaling.

questions.text: A teammate implements a causal mask by setting the scores of future positions to 0 before the softmax. What goes wrong?

options.text: The model crashes with a shape error
Nothing; 0 and -inf give identical weights
Future positions get zero weight, but so do all past positions
Softmax still gives future positions a non-zero weight, so the model quietly leaks information from the future

questions.explanation: A score of 0 is not neutral to softmax; it counts as moderately plausible. Only adding -inf makes exp(-inf) = 0 and gives masked positions exactly zero weight. The bug does not crash, which is why it is dangerous.

questions.text: Going from 1 attention head to 8 heads at the same d_model adds roughly eight times as many parameters.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Wq, Wk, Wv and Wo stay d_model x d_model whatever the head count. The heads are made by splitting the projected vectors, so the parameter count is unchanged and each head just works in a smaller subspace with its own softmax.

questions.text: Which statements about sampling the next token are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Top-k keeps exactly k candidate tokens, whether the model is confident or torn
Top-p keeps fewer tokens when one token holds most of the probability mass
Temperature removes low-probability tokens from consideration
Greedy decoding samples tokens in proportion to their probabilities

questions.explanation: Top-k is a fixed count while top-p adapts to the shape of the distribution. Temperature only reshapes the probabilities and removes nothing, and greedy decoding always takes the single most likely token rather than sampling.

questions.text: A batch pads shorter sequences with [PAD] tokens so they fit in one tensor. Which are true of masking in this setup? Select all that apply.

options.text: A padding mask stops real tokens from attending to the padding
A padding mask and a causal mask are applied by different mechanisms, so they cannot be combined
Both kinds of mask work by adding -inf to scores before the softmax
A causal mask also hides padding that comes before the real tokens, so no padding mask is needed

questions.explanation: Padding masks and causal masks are the same additive -inf tool aimed at different problems: one hides non-content, the other hides the future. They are commonly combined additively before a single softmax. A causal mask hides only future positions: padding placed before the real tokens (left padding) is in their past and stays visible, and an encoder with bidirectional attention has no causal mask at all, so a padding mask is still needed.

transactions-and-isolation-levels.title: Transactions, isolation and locking
transactions-and-isolation-levels.description: Read anomalies, PostgreSQL's isolation levels, pessimistic and optimistic locking, and how to avoid deadlocks.

questions.text: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level, and what does each statement see?

options.text: Serializable: every transaction runs as if alone
Repeatable Read: one snapshot for the whole transaction
Read Committed: each statement sees data committed before that statement began
Read Uncommitted: uncommitted changes are visible to everyone

questions.explanation: Read Committed prevents dirty reads but allows a later statement in the same transaction to see newly committed changes. The stronger levels must be requested explicitly.

questions.text: Inside one transaction you run SELECT ... WHERE status = 'open' twice. Between the runs another transaction inserts a matching row and commits, and your second run returns an extra row. Which anomaly is this?

options.text: Dirty read
Phantom read
Non-repeatable read
Lost update

questions.explanation: A phantom is a row appearing in (or vanishing from) a set matched by a predicate. A non-repeatable read is when an existing row you already read comes back with a different value. A dirty read involves uncommitted data.

questions.text: On PostgreSQL at Read Committed, an application that reads a balance, adds 10 in code and writes it back is safe from lost updates.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Two transactions can both read 100 and both write back their own result, so the second write overwrites the first. You need row locking, an atomic UPDATE, a version check, or a stronger isolation level with retries.

questions.text: Under PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ, two transactions update the same row. The first commits. What happens to the second?

options.text: It fails with a serialization error and must be retried
It silently overwrites the first update
It merges both updates automatically
It keeps waiting until the first transaction rolls back

questions.explanation: The second update blocks until the first finishes, then fails with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' because its snapshot is stale. The application has to catch that error and retry the whole transaction.

questions.text: Which approaches prevent a lost update when many requests change the same account balance? Select all that apply.

options.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before computing the new balance
An UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ? that is retried when it affects 0 rows
A single atomic statement such as UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10
A plain SELECT then UPDATE at Read Committed, with a short transaction

questions.explanation: Pessimistic locking, optimistic versioning and an atomic update each stop two writers from acting on the same stale value. A short transaction narrows the window but does not close it.

questions.text: Two code paths transfer money between accounts A and B. One locks A then B, the other locks B then A, and they occasionally deadlock. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Raise deadlock_timeout so transactions wait longer
Switch both paths to Read Uncommitted
Add more connections to the pool
Have every code path lock the rows in the same order, such as lowest id first

questions.explanation: A deadlock needs a cycle of waits, and a consistent lock order makes a cycle impossible. A longer timeout only delays detection, and PostgreSQL has no real Read Uncommitted anyway.

questions.text: With optimistic locking, your UPDATE ... WHERE id = 'A' AND version = 7 reports 0 rows affected. What does that mean?

options.text: The row does not exist, so you should insert it
The database lost the update; you should restart the server
Someone else changed the row first, so re-read it and retry
The write succeeded but nothing needed changing

questions.explanation: The version no longer matches because another transaction bumped it. The application must detect the zero-row result, re-read the fresh row and retry (the re-read also shows if the row was deleted instead). This only pays off when conflicts are rare.

questions.text: Several workers poll a jobs table, and you want each worker to claim different rows without waiting on each other. Which clause fits?

options.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
SELECT ... FOR SHARE
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE with no other clause
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE

questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED passes over rows another transaction already locked, so workers pick different rows. Plain FOR UPDATE makes every worker queue behind the first, and Serializable would produce errors to retry instead.

client-retries-with-backoff.title: Add retries with backoff to an API client
client-retries-with-backoff.brief:
Your service calls a partner's HTTP API to create shipping labels (`POST /labels`) and to look up their status (`GET /labels/{id}`). Today the client makes one attempt with a 60 second timeout. During busy hours the partner answers some calls with `429 Too Many Requests` (sometimes with a `Retry-After` header), occasionally with `502` or `503`, and a few requests just time out. The first quick fix someone proposed was "retry up to 10 times with no delay", which made an incident worse.

Design the retry behaviour of this client and write it down precisely enough that another engineer could implement it and test it. Pay attention to which calls are safe to repeat: a retried `POST /labels` after a timeout may create two labels if the first attempt actually succeeded. The partner supports an `Idempotency-Key` request header on `POST`.

The backoff formula with a base delay, a multiplier, a cap and jitter, and which jitter variant you chose and why
How a Retry-After header is honoured and how it combines with your own backoff
The maximum attempts and a total time budget for one logical call, and how this fits inside your own caller's timeout
How you make POST /labels safe to retry (idempotency key: when it is generated, that it is reused across attempts)
Timeouts per attempt (connect and read), and why 60 seconds is too long
A retry budget or circuit breaker so that many clients do not multiply load on a struggling partner
The logging and metrics you would add, and three test cases (including a fake server that fails twice then succeeds)

debug-slow-query-with-explain.title: Debug a slow query with EXPLAIN
debug-slow-query-with-explain.brief:
The "my shipped orders" page of an online shop takes about three seconds and the database CPU spikes when many customers open it. The database is PostgreSQL.

**Schema**

```sql

  id         bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  email      text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_key ON customers (email);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id),
  status      text   NOT NULL,           -- placed, paid, shipped, delivered, cancelled
  total_cents integer NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL
);
-- orders has about 20 million rows; a typical customer has under 200 of them
```

**Query 1 (the page)**

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242 AND status = 'shipped'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

```
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
 Limit  (cost=397604.25..397604.30 rows=20 width=48) (actual time=2810.40..2810.45 rows=20 loops=1)
   ->  Sort  (cost=397604.25..397604.54 rows=118 width=48) (actual time=2810.39..2810.42 rows=20 loops=1)
         Sort Key: created_at DESC

               Rows Removed by Filter: 19999904
 Planning Time: 0.15 ms
 Execution Time: 2810.60 ms
```


The exact CREATE INDEX statements, including how you build them without blocking writes on a busy table

Two things that would still make the first query slow after the index exists (for example SELECT * or a very low-selectivity filter) and what you would do about them

paginated-list-endpoint.title: Design a paginated, cache-friendly list endpoint
paginated-list-endpoint.brief:
A blog platform has an endpoint that returns articles:

```
GET /v1/articles?page=3&per_page=20&tag=python
```

It is implemented as `SELECT ... FROM articles WHERE tag = ? ORDER BY published_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40`. The table has 30 million rows and new articles are published every few seconds. Symptoms reported by users and the on-call engineer:

- Deep pages (page 5000 and beyond) take several seconds and load the database.
- A reader scrolling the list sees the same article twice, or misses one, when something new is published between two requests.
- The response is never cached by the CDN because every client sends different query strings and no caching headers are set.
- The endpoint returns a `total` count, and the `COUNT(*)` behind it is the slowest part of the request.

Redesign the endpoint. Write a short design document (and, if you like, a sketch of the handler and the SQL) that fixes all four symptoms without breaking existing clients more than necessary.

A migration path for clients that still send page and per_page
